# The Lodger at Number Seven

## Chapter 1

I first met Adrian Voss on a wet Tuesday in March. He was a consulting detective
who kept rooms at Number Seven, Grey Lane, two floors above a tobacconist's.
Voss was tall, thin, and restless; his eyes missed nothing. He played the violin
badly but with conviction, and he preferred black coffee to tea.

My name is Helen Carr. I am a physician lately returned from service overseas.
I keep a notebook of every case we share. Voss calls me "Carr" in company and
"my dear Carr" when we are alone. The neighbours know him simply as Voss; the
papers call him Adrian Voss, the detective of Grey Lane.

## Chapter 2

Mrs. Bramley owns the house at Number Seven. She is sixty, widowed, and keeps
three cats. She believes Voss never sleeps. That is not quite true: he sleeps
in short spells after a case closes. He keeps a worn leather case of chemicals
on the mantel and a map of the city pinned above his desk.

One morning a client arrived — a banker named Oswald Trent from the firm of
Trent & Wilde. Trent reported that a sealed letter had vanished from his office
safe. He believed a clerk named Mina Cole had taken it. Voss doubted that at
once. "Cole has no motive," he said. "Look to the partner instead."

## Chapter 3

We found the letter behind a loose brick in Wilde's private study. Wilde had
lied about being out of town. Voss confronted him with the brick dust still on
his cuffs. Wilde confessed that he owed money to a faction calling itself the
Amber Circle. The Amber Circle meets above a bookshop in Harbour Street.

Carr recorded the confession in her notebook before the constable arrived.
Voss returned to Number Seven and played the violin until dawn. Mrs. Bramley
left a tray of cold toast outside his door and pretended not to hear.
